etymology: The Black American pronunciation of sucker, which in 19th-century American English meant a dupe, a greenhorn, an easy mark (probably from sucker, a young animal not yet weaned). Sucka was at home in African-American speech and 1970s film long before it went national, and the Keenen Ivory Wayans comedy I’m Gonna Git You Sucka (1988) affectionately parodied the films that had used it. It became a household taunt through Mr. T, whose B. A. Baracus on NBC’s The A-Team (1983–87) growled sucka and fool at the villains every week, a year after his Clubber Lang in Rocky III (1982) gave the country "I pity the fool."
biblical_def: Sucka is the playground word for a dupe: the kid who fell for the trick, the mark who paid too much, the bad guy who walked straight into the A-Team’s trap. When Mr. T growled it at a villain, it meant "you got played, and you had it coming." The word carries two things at once: a warning against being gullible and a sneer at those who are. Scripture keeps the warning and refuses the sneer. Proverbs has its own word for the sucka: the simple. "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15); "A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished" (Pro 22:3). Paul warns of men who "by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple" (Rom 16:18), and he wants believers to be "no more children, tossed to and fro" by the sleight of men (Eph 4:14). Our Lord sends His disciples out "wise as serpents, and harmless as doves" (Mat 10:16) — not easy marks, and not con men either. But the same Lord forbids the contempt: "whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire" (Mat 5:22). Wisdom calls the simple to come and learn (Pro 1:22); she does not mock them. A father can tell his son: don’t be a sucka — test what you hear, read the fine print, and know the Word well enough to spot a counterfeit. And when you see another boy get played, don’t sneer. Help him up; you were simple once too.
webster_summary: Black American pronunciation of sucker (a dupe, an easy mark), made a national taunt by Mr. T on The A-Team (1983); Scripture warns against being the simple who believeth every word (Pro 14:15) but forbids the sneer of "Thou fool" (Mat 5:22).
webster_full: SUCKA, n. and interj. (Gen X slang, 1970s–80s, African-American speech; national via The A-Team, 1983) A dupe, a chump, an easy mark; a taunt thrown at a beaten opponent. "You just got played, sucka."
From American sucker, a greenhorn or dupe (19th c.); compare sucker punch; the dropped -r reflects Black American pronunciation.
Companion taunts: fool, chump; Mr. T’s "I pity the fool" (Rocky III, 1982); parodied in I’m Gonna Git You Sucka (1988).
Webster 1828: SUCKER, n. He or that which draws with the mouth. …
Decode for parents: the word warns against being gullible and sneers at the gullible; keep the warning, drop the sneer.
scriptures: The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
Pro 22:3
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
corruption_summary: Sucka rightly warns against being easily played but turns the warning into contempt; Scripture calls the simple to wisdom and forbids the man who says, Thou fool.
corruption_paragraphs: Contempt for the conned. In the world of the taunt, the con man is clever and the mark is a loser — the blame quietly slides from the deceiver to the deceived. Scripture never makes that move. Paul denounces the men who "deceive the hearts of the simple" (Rom 16:18); he does not laugh at the simple. A boy raised on sucka can learn to admire the hustle and despise the hustled, and that is exactly backwards. Our Lord set a guard over the mouth: "Thou fool," spoken in contempt, is a matter for judgment (Mat 5:22).

Wise, not cynical. The cure for gullibility is not cynicism but prudence. The prudent man "looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15) and "foreseeth the evil" (Pro 22:3); the believer is "wise as serpents, and harmless as doves" (Mat 10:16). A Christian ought to be the hardest man in the room to con — because he knows the Word, counts the cost, and is not hungry for the easy deal — and the gentlest man in the room toward the one who got conned. Wisdom stands in the street and calls the simple home (Pro 1:22).
roots_summary: Old English sucan (to suck) → sucker, an unweaned young animal → 19th-c. American sucker (a dupe) → Black American sucka → Mr. T, The A-Team (1983); Scripture: the simple believeth every word (Pro 14:15).
roots_lines: Old English sucan — to suck; sucker, a young animal not yet weaned
19th-c. American sucker — a greenhorn, a dupe, an easy mark
African-American pronunciation sucka; 1970s film and street speech
1982–83: Mr. T in Rocky III and The A-Team makes it a national taunt
Proverbs’ word for the sucka: the simple (Pro 14:15; Pro 22:3)
usage: "Nice try, sucka!" — every backyard, c. 1984.
The simple believeth every word (Pro 14:15); the prudent reads the fine print.
Don’t be the mark, and don’t mock the mark (Mat 5:22).

etymology: Chick for a young woman is American slang of the 1920s (from chicken, a young person); flick for a motion picture is of the same decade, from the flicker of early film. The rhyming compound chick flick was in American use by the late 1980s and in everyone’s mouth by the early 1990s, attached to romances and tearjerkers marketed chiefly to women: Beaches (1988), Steel Magnolias (1989), Sleepless in Seattle (1993). It was usually said by a husband or boyfriend, with a sigh, on the way into the theater.
biblical_def: A chick flick is a movie made for women — romance, tears, friendship, a wedding near the end — and the word is usually said by a husband with a sigh as he is led to one. The phrase is half joke and half complaint, and it tells the truth about something: the film industry learned to sell longing. The Christian observation is that the longing is not the problem. God made it. The Song of Solomon is the Bible’s own love song, and it says "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it" (Son 8:7). What Scripture adds is order and patience: "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). Desire is a fire for the hearth of marriage, not a thing to be fanned for an evening’s entertainment. The danger of a steady diet of screen romance is that it trains a girl to wait for a script and a boy to think love is a feeling that happens to people rather than a covenant men keep. The Bible’s love story is better than Hollywood’s: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Eph 5:25). Real love "suffereth long, and is kind" (1Co 13:4); it can still "rejoice with the wife of thy youth" (Pro 5:18) forty years after the credits. A father can watch the movie with his daughter and then tell her the truth: the best love story is not the one where a stranger sweeps you off your feet, but the one where a man lays down his life for his bride — the story Christ wrote first.
webster_summary: Gen X slang (late 1980s–90s) for a romantic film marketed to women; Scripture honors the longing — many waters cannot quench love (Son 8:7) — and shows its true shape in a husband who gives himself as Christ did (Eph 5:25).
webster_full: CHICK FLICK, n. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, American) A motion picture, usually a romance or tearjerker, made and marketed chiefly for women. "You picked last time — no more chick flicks."
Rhyming compound of chick (a young woman, 1920s slang) and flick (a film, 1920s, from the flicker of early projection).
Counterparts: guy movie, dude flick; kin to tearjerker, weepie, rom-com.
Webster 1828: CHICKEN, n. 1. The young of fowls, particularly of the domestic hen, or gallinaceous fowls. 2. A person of tender years. …
Decode for parents: the longing these films sell is real and God-given; teach children that love is a covenant kept, not a feeling that happens to them.
scriptures: Son 8:7
Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
Son 2:7
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
Pro 5:18
Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.
corruption_summary: The chick flick sells a real, God-given longing in a script that ends at the wedding; Scripture shows love as a covenant kept long after the credits roll.
corruption_paragraphs: Romance as a product. Hollywood discovered that longing could be packaged, and the result was a genre that wakes desire on a schedule: two hours of stirring up, a kiss, the credits. The Shulamite’s refrain runs the other way — "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). A girl fed on the formula can come to measure a real husband against a scripted one and find him dull; a boy can conclude that love is lightning rather than labor. Neither lesson is in the Song of Solomon.

The better story. Scripture does not sneer at romance; it puts a whole love song in the canon (Son 8:7). But it finishes the story Hollywood stops telling: the husband who loves his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it (Eph 5:25), the charity that suffereth long (1Co 13:4), the man who still rejoices with the wife of his youth (Pro 5:18) when both are gray. The sneer in the name — that such stories are only for women — misses the point too: covenant love is a man’s work first.
roots_summary: Chicken → 1920s chick (young woman) + 1920s flick (film) → chick flick (late 1980s–90s romances); Scripture: love that many waters cannot quench, kept in covenant (Son 8:7; Eph 5:25).
roots_lines: Old English cicen — a young fowl; chick, a young bird
1920s American slang: chick, a young woman; the flicks, the movies
Late 1980s–1990s: chick flick for romances and tearjerkers marketed to women
Beaches (1988), Steel Magnolias (1989), Sleepless in Seattle (1993) set the type
Scripture’s love story: the Song of Solomon (Son 8:7) and Christ and His church (Eph 5:25)
usage: "Your turn to pick? Fine, but no chick flicks."
Stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please (Son 2:7) — the Bible’s word to the movie-night romantic.
The best love story ends not at the wedding but at the cross (Eph 5:25).

etymology: From the riot grrrl punk scene of the early 1990s in Olympia, Washington, and Washington, D.C., where the band Bikini Kill and its photocopied zines used girl power as a rallying cry (c. 1991). The British pop group the Spice Girls took it worldwide in 1996–97 with their debut single "Wannabe" and a flood of interviews and merchandise; by 1997 girl power was printed on T-shirts and lunchboxes. The phrase names a cheerful, market-friendly feminism of female confidence, friendship, and independence.
biblical_def: Girl power was the slogan of the late 1990s: a lunchbox, a T-shirt, a Spice Girls chorus, and the message to a little girl that she could be strong, loud, and anything she wanted. Behind the merchandise was a real question every daughter asks: is there strength for me, and where does it come from? Scripture answers yes, and then answers better than the slogan. The Bible is full of strong women: Deborah, who arose "a mother in Israel" when the men faltered (Jdg 5:7); Esther, told she had come to the kingdom "for such a time as this" (Est 4:14); the virtuous woman who "girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms" (Pro 31:17), of whom it is said, "Strength and honour are her clothing" (Pro 31:25). But Scripture never locates the power in the girl. "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God" (Psa 62:11). Deborah’s strength was God’s deliverance; Esther’s courage was obedience at the risk of her life. And the strongest thing Paul ever learned was that God’s "strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). A slogan that tells a girl to look inward for power will fail her on her worst day, because the well runs dry. A father can tell his daughter: you are not weak, and you were not made to be a decoration — but your strength is borrowed, and the Lender is faithful. Be a Deborah, not a brand.
webster_summary: Riot grrrl rallying cry (c. 1991) taken worldwide by the Spice Girls (1996–97) for female confidence and independence; Scripture honors strong women like Deborah and the virtuous wife but says power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11).
webster_full: GIRL POWER, n. (Gen X slang, early 1990s riot grrrl; mainstream 1996–97 via the Spice Girls) Female confidence, solidarity, and independence, as a slogan or cheer. "Girl power!"
Roots in the Olympia, Washington, punk scene (Bikini Kill and its zines, c. 1991); spelled grrrl in the underground.
Mainstreamed as merchandise in the "Wannabe" years: T-shirts, lunchboxes, dolls; later a staple of advertising.

Webster 1828: POWER, n. [The Latin has posse, possum, potes, potentia. The primary sense of the verb is to strain, to exert force.] 1. In a philosophical sense, the faculty of doing or performing any thing; the faculty of moving or of producing a change in something; ability or strength. …
Decode for parents: the slogan answers a daughter’s real question about strength; Scripture answers it better — strength from God, spent in His service.
scriptures: God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God.
She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms.
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
Jdg 5:7
The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Girl power tells a daughter that strength is hers to summon from within; Scripture clothes a woman in strength and honour but locates all power in God, made perfect in weakness.
corruption_paragraphs: Power from within. The slogan’s premise is that a girl’s strength is already inside her, waiting to be believed in. It sells well and wears thin. Every girl meets the day when confidence runs out — a loss, a sin, a betrayal — and a creed of self-power has nothing to say to her then. The Psalmist heard God speak twice on the matter: "power belongeth unto God" (Psa 62:11). Paul learned it in his own weakness: "my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). That is a word for daughters and sons alike.

The strong women of Scripture. The church has no reason to answer the slogan with a shrug, as if godly women were meant to be feeble. Deborah judged Israel and arose a mother in Israel (Jdg 5:7); the virtuous woman girds her loins with strength (Pro 31:17) and wears strength and honour as her clothing (Pro 31:25). Their strength served God, their households, and their people, not a brand. A daughter who learns that will be stronger than any slogan, and freer than any lunchbox promised.
roots_summary: Latin posse → Old French poer → English power; riot grrrl girl power (Olympia, c. 1991) → Spice Girls (1996–97) → slogan and merchandise; Scripture: power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11).
roots_lines: Latin posse — to be able; Old French poer → English power
c. 1991: riot grrrl punk scene, Olympia and Washington, D.C.; Bikini Kill
1996–97: the Spice Girls make girl power a worldwide pop slogan
Late 1990s: T-shirts, lunchboxes, advertising copy
Scripture’s strong women: Deborah (Jdg 5:7), the virtuous woman (Pro 31:25); the source: God (Psa 62:11)
usage: "Girl power!" — printed on a 1997 lunchbox.
Strength and honour are her clothing (Pro 31:25) — strength worn, not manufactured.
Power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11), and He perfects it in weakness (2Co 12:9).

etymology: From wedge, for the way the prank drives the victim’s underwear up like a wedge. American schoolyard slang in use by the 1970s and universal in the 1980s, when the wedgie became a stock gag of school comedies and Saturday cartoons; escalated forms such as the atomic wedgie followed. A milder sense, clothing that has bunched up by accident, is also current.
biblical_def: A wedgie is the prank of grabbing a boy’s underwear from behind and yanking it upward — usually in a locker room or hallway, usually by a bigger kid, usually to laughter. For Gen X boys it was a rite of passage, a cartoon gag, and for some a daily dread. The Christian observation is that the prank’s whole pleasure is humiliation: exposing and shaming someone weaker in front of an audience. Scripture has an old story about exactly that. When Noah lay uncovered in his tent, Ham "saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without" (Gen 9:22) — he made a joke of another man’s shame. His brothers did the opposite: they "took a garment, and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father" (Gen 9:23). That is the Christian instinct: cover, don’t expose. "We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves" (Rom 15:1). The golden rule settles the locker room: "all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them" (Mat 7:12). Proverbs has no patience for cruelty dressed as fun; it likens the man who wounds his neighbour and then says "Am not I in sport?" to a madman who "casteth firebrands, arrows, and death" (Pro 26:18). A father can tell his son: never be the one who pulls it, and when you see it happen, be Shem — step in and cover your brother. That is what Christ did for us, bearing our shame so ours could be covered.
webster_summary: Schoolyard prank (US, by the 1970s; ubiquitous in the 1980s) of yanking a victim’s underwear upward from behind; humiliation for an audience, against which Scripture sets Shem and Japheth covering their father’s shame (Gen 9:23).
webster_full: WEDGIE, n. (Gen X slang, 1970s–80s, American schoolyard) The prank of seizing a person’s underwear from behind and jerking it upward. "The eighth-graders gave him a wedgie at the bus stop."
From wedge; escalated forms atomic wedgie, hanging wedgie; also as a verb, to wedgie.
Milder sense: clothing accidentally bunched up; a stock gag of 1980s school comedies and cartoons.
Webster 1828: WEDGE, n. [This word signifies a mass, a lump.] 1. A mass of metal; as a wedge of gold or silver. Joshua 7:21. …
Decode for parents: the prank’s fun is another boy’s humiliation; teach your son to be the one who covers, not the one who exposes.
scriptures: Gen 9:22
And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without.
Gen 9:23

And Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness.
Rom 15:1
We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Mat 7:12
Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death,
corruption_summary: The wedgie makes a laugh out of a weaker boy’s shame; Scripture blesses the brothers who covered their father’s nakedness and calls the strong to bear the infirmities of the weak.
corruption_paragraphs: Cruelty as comedy. The 1980s treated the wedgie as harmless horseplay, and between equal friends it may be. But the classic wedgie runs downhill: the big kid, the small kid, the crowd. Its pleasure is exposure. Proverbs compares the man who wounds his neighbour and then says he was only joking to a madman throwing firebrands (Pro 26:18). The laugh does not cancel the wound; it adds to it. A culture that files bullying under "boys will be boys" has forgotten that the strong are accountable for how they use their strength (Rom 15:1).

Ham or Shem. Genesis 9 sets the two responses side by side. Ham saw his father’s shame and told it for a laugh (Gen 9:22); Shem and Japheth walked backward with a garment and covered it (Gen 9:23). Every schoolboy will stand in that hallway sooner or later, and he will be one brother or the other. The gospel makes Christians coverers by nature: Christ bore our shame openly so that ours could be covered, and those who know it cannot enjoy exposing a brother.
roots_summary: Old English wecg → wedge → American schoolyard wedgie (by the 1970s) → 1980s stock gag; Scripture: cover the shame of the weak (Gen 9:23; Rom 15:1).
roots_lines: Old English wecg — a wedge, a piece of metal or wood driven into a cleft
By the 1970s: American schoolyard wedgie, underwear driven up like a wedge
1980s: a stock gag of school comedies and Saturday cartoons
Escalations: atomic wedgie, hanging wedgie
Biblical counter-pattern: Ham exposes (Gen 9:22); Shem and Japheth cover (Gen 9:23)
usage: "Watch out for Biff — he gives wedgies in the locker room."
The strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak (Rom 15:1), not hoist them by the waistband.
Be Shem: take a garment and cover your brother (Gen 9:23).

etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps a childish alteration of knuckle; American slang for a hard rub of the knuckles on someone’s scalp, in use by the 1960s. Gen X learned it from Saturday Night Live’s "The Nerds" sketches (1978–80), in which Bill Murray’s Todd DiLaMuca administered noogies to Gilda Radner’s Lisa Loopner. In family life it is the natural finish of the big-brother headlock.
biblical_def: A noogie is the hard knuckle-rub on the top of the head, delivered from inside a headlock, usually by a big brother, an uncle, or a coach, usually with a grin. It hurts a little and means a lot: it is how many boys were told, without words, that they belonged. The Christian observation is that rough affection is a real thing, and Scripture is not squeamish about it. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6). Brothers are made for hard days: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17). The backyard headlock is a small picture of how "good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity" (Psa 133:1). But affection that is rough must stay affection. The line is the one Paul draws for fathers: "provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged" (Col 3:21). A noogie that ends in laughter is brotherly love; a noogie that ends in tears and keeps going has become something else. "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love" (Rom 12:10), and when the play goes too far, be "tenderhearted, forgiving one another" (Eph 4:32). A father can give his son a noogie and teach him in the same breath: strength in a family is for play and protection, never for making the little one cry, and the strongest one in the room should always be the first to stop.
webster_summary: American slang (by the 1960s; popularized by SNL’s "The Nerds," 1978–80) for a knuckle-rub on the scalp, the big brother’s rough affection; Scripture honors the faithful wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6) and draws the line at provoking to anger (Col 3:21).
webster_full: NOOGIE, n. (Gen X slang, American; popular late 1970s–80s) A hard rubbing of the knuckles on another’s scalp, usually from a headlock, as teasing or rough affection. "Come here, squirt — noogie time!"
Origin uncertain, perhaps from knuckle; plural noogies; nearly always paired with the headlock.
Fixed in Gen X memory by Bill Murray and Gilda Radner’s "The Nerds" on Saturday Night Live (1978–80).
No entry in Webster 1828; noogie is 20th-century American slang of uncertain origin.
Decode for parents: rough affection is real affection when it ends in laughter; teach the strongest child to be the first to stop.
scriptures: Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Col 3:21
Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.
Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
corruption_summary: The noogie is rough affection that can slide into domination; Scripture honors the faithful wounds of a friend and brotherly love, and forbids provoking the little ones to anger.
corruption_paragraphs: When play turns. Most noogies are love in disguise, and men who grew up with brothers know it. But the same headlock that says "you belong" can, held a few seconds too long, say "I can do what I want with you." The difference is not in the knuckles but in the heart behind them, and children feel it instantly. Paul’s word to fathers draws the line for every older brother too: provoke not to anger, lest they be discouraged (Col 3:21). Strength that will not stop when the little one is crying has stopped being play.

Faithful wounds. The Bible does not want families made of porcelain. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" (Pro 27:6): a brother who will wrestle you, tease you, and tell you the truth is worth more than a flatterer. A brother is "born for adversity" (Pro 17:17), and the boys who roughhoused in the backyard are often the men who stand together at a graveside. Keep the noogie; keep it kind (Rom 12:10), and when it goes too far, be quick to say sorry and quicker to forgive (Eph 4:32).
roots_summary: Uncertain origin (perhaps knuckle) → American noogie (by the 1960s) → SNL’s "The Nerds" (1978–80) → the big-brother headlock; Scripture: a brother is born for adversity (Pro 17:17).
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; perhaps a childish alteration of knuckle
By the 1960s: American slang for a knuckle-rub on the scalp
1978–80: SNL’s "The Nerds" (Bill Murray, Gilda Radner) make it famous
1980s: the headlock-and-noogie, standard household rough play
Biblical rough love: faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6)
usage: "Mom! He’s giving me noogies again!"
A brother is born for adversity (Pro 17:17) — and now and then for noogies.
Fathers, provoke not your children to anger (Col 3:21): the strongest stops first.

etymology: From jynx, the wryneck, a bird the ancient Greeks bound to a wheel in love-charms (Greek iynx), hence a charm or spell. Jinx for a person or thing that brings bad luck is American slang by about 1910, common in baseball writing. For Gen X children it was also a schoolyard game: when two people say the same word at the same moment, the first to shout "Jinx!" silences the other until his name is spoken — or, by the common rule, until he is bought a Coke.
biblical_def: Jinx has two lives in Gen X memory. On the playground it was a game: two kids say the same thing at the same time, one yells "Jinx! You owe me a Coke!" and the other must stay silent until someone speaks his name. At the ballgame and on the school bus it was a superstition: don’t mention the no-hitter, you’ll jinx it; don’t say we’ll win, you’ll jinx us. The game is harmless fun. The superstition is worth a closer look, because the word comes from the jynx, a bird the Greeks used in spells. To fear a jinx is to believe that words or luck can bend events apart from God. Scripture answers that fear with a Sovereign. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33). Balaam, hired to curse Israel, discovered that "there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel" (Num 23:23). The Lord "frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad" (Isa 44:25), and He tells His people, "Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven" (Jer 10:2). Not one sparrow falls "without your Father" (Mat 10:29). A father can play jinx at the dinner table and laugh about the Coke; then, when the team is up in the ninth and someone whispers "don’t jinx it," he can smile and say: nobody can jinx what God has ordained. Speak freely; the Lord holds the game.
webster_summary: From the jynx, a bird used in Greek charms, through American baseball slang (c. 1910) for a bringer of bad luck, to the schoolyard game of simultaneous speech; Scripture answers the superstition: the whole disposing of the lot is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).
webster_full: JINX, n., interj., and v. (Gen X schoolyard slang; American from c. 1910) A person, thing, or word thought to bring bad luck; as an interjection, the call in the game of simultaneous speech. "Jinx! You owe me a Coke!" "Don’t say it — you’ll jinx it."
The game: whoever calls "Jinx!" first silences the other until his name is spoken; local rules vary on how the silence is lifted.
Superstition sense: to jinx a winning streak by speaking of it; jinxed, dogged by bad luck; a fixture of sports and theater lore.
No entry in Webster 1828 for jinx or its likely source jynx (the wryneck bird of Greek charm-magic); the word entered American slang in the early 20th century.
Decode for parents: play the game, but teach that no word or omen can jinx what God has ordained.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Surely there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel: according to this time it shall be said of Jacob and of Israel, What hath God wrought!
That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish;
Jer 10:2
Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them.
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
corruption_summary: Jinx keeps alive, in a child’s game and a fan’s fear, the old belief that words and omens can bend events; Scripture answers with a God who disposes every lot and against whose people there is no enchantment.
corruption_paragraphs: The superstition under the game. The playground jinx is a test of quick reflexes and nothing more. The ballpark jinx is something else: the quiet belief that saying a thing aloud can spoil it, that luck is a force with a will of its own. That belief is a small piece of paganism wearing a ball cap. Its root is literal — the Greek wryneck bound to a wheel in love-spells — and its logic is the logic of the heathen who are "dismayed at the signs of heaven" (Jer 10:2). The Christian has no reason to be dismayed.

No enchantment against Jacob. Balaam was paid to speak a curse over Israel and could not make it stick: "there is no enchantment against Jacob" (Num 23:23). The lot falls into the lap, but the LORD disposes it (Pro 16:33); He frustrates the tokens of liars (Isa 44:25); not a sparrow falls without the Father (Mat 10:29). A child who knows this can say "we’re going to win" and lose without fear, because nothing he said changed anything God decreed. Providence is the end of superstition.
roots_summary: Greek iynx (the wryneck, a charm-bird) → Latin and English jynx → American jinx (c. 1910, baseball) → the schoolyard game; Scripture: the disposing of the lot is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).
roots_lines: Greek iynx — the wryneck, bound to a wheel in ancient love-charms
Latin and English jynx — the wryneck; hence a charm or spell
c. 1910: American baseball slang jinx, a bringer of bad luck
1970s–80s playground game: "Jinx! You owe me a Coke!"
Biblical answer: no enchantment against Jacob (Num 23:23); the lot is the LORD’s (Pro 16:33)
usage: "Jinx! You owe me a Coke!"
Don’t worry about jinxing it: the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).
There is no enchantment against Jacob (Num 23:23) — nor against the children of God.

etymology: From riding shotgun, the armed guard who sat beside the stagecoach driver with a shotgun across his knees in the American West; the phrase was spread by Western fiction and films of the early 20th century. Later in the century teenagers turned it into a seat-claim: the first to shout "Shotgun!" wins the front passenger seat. In the Gen X station-wagon years the call came with unwritten rules — the car must be in sight, no calling it from inside the house — that every sibling could recite.
biblical_def: To call shotgun is to shout the word before anyone else and claim the front seat of the car. In Gen X families it was law: the first to yell it got the seat, and siblings argued the fine points like lawyers — do you have to see the car? does it count from the porch? The word is innocent; the scramble behind it is very old. The disciples called shotgun on the kingdom. James and John came to Jesus and asked, "Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory" (Mar 10:37), and the other ten were indignant, very likely because they had not called it first. Jesus answered with a different seating rule: "whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister" (Mat 20:26), and "whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant" (Mat 20:27). At a feast He told men to "go and sit down in the lowest room" and wait to be invited higher (Luk 14:10). "If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all" (Mar 9:35). Paul turns it into a habit of mind: "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Php 2:3). A family can keep the game — it settles arguments fast — but a father can also teach the better move. Now and then, let your son win shotgun and hand it to his little sister, or to Grandma, without being asked. That is the kingdom’s seating chart, and the Lord Himself took the lowest seat of all.
webster_summary: The call that claims the front passenger seat, from the Old West’s riding shotgun; a harmless family rule over a very old scramble for the best seat, which Jesus answered by making the chief the servant of all (Mat 20:27).
webster_full: SHOTGUN, interj. and n. (Gen X slang, American; universal 1970s–80s) A call claiming the front passenger seat of a car; the seat itself. "Shotgun!" "No fair — you had shotgun last time."
From riding shotgun, the stagecoach guard seated beside the driver with a shotgun; spread by Western fiction and film.
Family case law: the car must be in sight; no calling it from indoors; the loser rides in the back of the station wagon.
No entry in Webster 1828; shotgun is a 19th-century American word, and the seat-claim is 20th-century slang.
Decode for parents: the game settles arguments; the kingdom teaches a child to give the best seat away.
scriptures: They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:

But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
corruption_summary: Shotgun is a harmless game over a very old appetite — the scramble for the best seat — which Jesus answered by putting the servant at the head of the table.
corruption_paragraphs: The scramble for the seat. Nothing is wrong with a family rule that ends arguments before they start. But the game exercises a muscle every child already has too much of: the reflex to grab the best place first. The disciples had it on the road to Jerusalem, asking for the seats at Christ’s right and left hand (Mar 10:37) while He was speaking of His death. Grown men have it in boardrooms, churches, and committee meetings. The Lord’s cure was not a ban on seats but a new definition of greatness (Mat 20:26-27).

Friend, go up higher. Jesus told His hearers to take the lowest room and let the host call them up (Luk 14:10). Paul made it a rule of the mind: esteem others better than yourself (Php 2:3). A boy who learns to give up shotgun to his grandmother is learning the posture of the Son of God, who did not grasp at the highest place but took the form of a servant. That lesson will serve him longer than any front seat.
roots_summary: Old West riding shotgun (the stagecoach guard) → Western fiction and film → teenage seat-claim → Gen X family law; Scripture: whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant (Mat 20:27).
roots_lines: 19th-c. American shotgun — a smoothbore gun firing shot
Old West: the guard riding shotgun beside the stagecoach driver
Early 20th c.: the phrase spreads through Western fiction and films
Later 20th c.: "Shotgun!" claims the front passenger seat; family rules multiply
The kingdom’s seating chart: the lowest room (Luk 14:10); the servant of all (Mar 9:35)
usage: "Shotgun!" "You can’t call it till we’re outside!"
James and John called shotgun on the kingdom (Mar 10:37); Jesus answered with the servant’s seat (Mat 20:27).
Sit down in the lowest room (Luk 14:10) — and let the Host call you higher.

etymology: The haircut — short on the top and sides, long in the back — was everywhere in the 1980s and early 1990s, from hockey rinks to country music (Billy Ray Cyrus, "Achy Breaky Heart," 1992) to prime-time television. It had no settled name until the Beastie Boys named it in their song "Mullet Head" (1994), drawing on the old American insult mullethead, a dull, thick-headed fellow. The catchphrase "business in the front, party in the back" followed later in the 1990s. The older English mullet is the fish.
biblical_def: The mullet is the haircut Gen X would rather forget and cannot: short in front, long in back, "business in the front, party in the back." It crowned hockey players, country singers, and half the yearbook in 1987. The name came late, after its heyday, from a 1994 Beastie Boys song and an old insult for a dull fellow — a sign the culture had already begun laughing at it. The Christian observation is gentle: hairstyles come and go, and the Bible is not a style guide. "The very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Mat 10:30); God cares about the man under the hair far more than its cut. Still, Scripture has one famous haircut story, and it is a warning. Absalom was the most praised man in Israel "for his beauty: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him" (2Sa 14:25), and he weighed his yearly trimmings like treasure. In the end, riding in rebellion against his father, "his head caught hold of the oak" (2Sa 18:9), and the glory he was proud of held him fast for his enemies. Pride in appearance is a slow trap. Peter points to a better adornment than any style: "the hidden man of the heart" and "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4). The only hairstyle Proverbs praises is gray: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31). A father can pull out the old photos and laugh with his kids. Then he can tell them: the cut will date you; the heart is what God sees.
webster_summary: The 1980s haircut, short in front and long in back, named after its heyday by the Beastie Boys’ "Mullet Head" (1994); a harmless fashion with a quiet warning from Absalom, whose proud head caught hold of the oak (2Sa 18:9).
webster_full: MULLET, n. (Gen X slang, named 1994; the style itself 1980s–early 1990s) A haircut cropped short on the top and sides and left long at the back. "Look at Uncle Rick’s mullet in the 1988 family photo."
Named by the Beastie Boys’ "Mullet Head" (1994), from the American insult mullethead, a dull fellow; catchphrase "business in the front, party in the back."
Associated with hockey, country music (Billy Ray Cyrus, 1992), and 1980s television; revived ironically in the 2010s–20s.

Webster 1828: MULLET, n. [Latin mullus.] A fish of the genus Mugil. The lips are membranaceous; the inferior one carinated inwards; it has no teeth, and the body is of a whitish color. This fish frequents the shore and roots in the sand like a hog. It is an excellent fish for the table.
Decode for parents: laugh at the old photos together; teach that God numbers the hairs and looks on the heart.
scriptures: But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
But in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

And Absalom met the servants of David. And Absalom rode upon a mule, and the mule went under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head caught hold of the oak, and he was taken up between the heaven and the earth; and the mule that was under him went away.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
corruption_summary: The mullet is a harmless fashion now worn mostly as a joke; Scripture neither condemns nor commends a haircut, but warns through Absalom that pride in one’s looks is a trap.
corruption_paragraphs: Fashion and its expiration date. The mullet is the clearest proof that appearance is a moving target: the cut that looked sharp in 1987 looked ridiculous by 1997, and its very name was an insult. Children who page through the old yearbooks learn a useful lesson early: the world’s idea of good-looking changes every decade, so it is a poor foundation for a life. "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). A haircut can be laughed at; a heart has to be tended.

Absalom’s hair. Scripture’s one great haircut story is about pride. Absalom was praised from sole to crown (2Sa 14:25) and weighed his trimmings each year, and the glory he cultivated caught in an oak and held him for the spears (2Sa 18:9). The point is not that long hair is wicked; it is that what a man is proud of can become what holds him. Peter’s adornment — the meek and quiet spirit, of great price in God’s sight (1Pe 3:4) — never goes out of style.
roots_summary: Latin mullus → English mullet (the fish) → American mullethead (a dullard) → Beastie Boys’ "Mullet Head" (1994) names the 1980s haircut; Scripture: the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
roots_lines: Latin mullus → Old French mulet → English mullet, the fish
19th-c. American mullethead — a dull, thick-headed person
1980s–early 1990s: the short-front, long-back haircut, unnamed at its peak
1994: the Beastie Boys’ "Mullet Head" gives the style its name
Biblical hair: numbered by God (Mat 10:30); Absalom’s pride caught in the oak (2Sa 18:9)
usage: "Business in the front, party in the back."
The very hairs of your head are all numbered (Mat 10:30) — even the ones in the back.
Absalom’s glory caught in an oak (2Sa 18:9); the hidden man of the heart is of great price (1Pe 3:4).

etymology: American, from fanny, informal US English for the backside (early 20th century), and pack. Belt pouches had long served skiers, hikers, and cyclists; the zippered nylon fanny pack became a mass fashion item in the mid-to-late 1980s, the uniform of tourists, theme-park parents, and mall walkers, and a byword for unfashionable practicality by the late 1990s. In Britain it is called a bum bag, since fanny is impolite there. It returned in the 2010s as the belt bag.
biblical_def: The fanny pack was the 1980s answer to a simple problem: where do you keep your wallet, keys, sunscreen, and gum when you are walking all day? Strap a zippered pouch around your waist and your hands are free and your treasure is right in front of you. By the 1990s it was the punchline of every tourist joke. The Christian observation is that the Bible has a good deal to say about bags. David went out to meet Goliath with five smooth stones in "a shepherd’s bag which he had, even in a scrip" (1Sa 17:40) — a waist pouch carrying a great faith. Jesus sent out the seventy with orders to "Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes" (Luk 10:4), so they would learn the Father provides. Haggai describes the frustrated worker who "earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6) — money that leaks away because God is not first. And the Lord commands a different kind of pack entirely: "provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not" (Luk 12:33). The fanny pack keeps valuables close and in sight, which is exactly the instinct Jesus redirects: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Mat 6:21). A father can laugh at the photo of himself at the theme park in 1989 with a neon pouch around his middle; then he can ask his children what they keep closest, and whether it is the kind of bag that waxes old.
webster_summary: American name (from fanny, the backside) for the zippered waist pouch of the mid-to-late 1980s, the tourist’s uniform and later a fashion joke; Scripture asks what we carry close, and bids us provide bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33).
webster_full: FANNY PACK, n. (Gen X slang, American; mass fashion mid-to-late 1980s) A small zippered pouch worn on a belt around the waist, for keys, money, and snacks. "The tickets are in my fanny pack."
From US informal fanny, the backside, + pack; British bum bag, since fanny is impolite there.
Earlier a skier’s and hiker’s belt pouch; revived in the 2010s as the belt bag or sling.

Webster 1828: PACK, n. [See the Verb.] 1. A bundle of any thing inclosed in a cover or bound fast with cords; a bale; as a pack of goods or cloth. The soldier bears a pack on his back. 2. A burden or load; as a pack of sorrows. …
Decode for parents: the fanny pack keeps treasure close; ask your children what treasure they keep closest.
scriptures: And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine.
Luk 10:4
Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes: and salute no man by the way.
Hag 1:6

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
Mat 6:21
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
corruption_summary: The fanny pack is a harmless convenience that became a fashion joke; Scripture uses bags and purses to ask the deeper question — what treasure we keep close, and whether the bag has holes.
corruption_paragraphs: The bag with holes. Haggai’s people worked hard and stayed poor; their wages went into "a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6) because they built their own houses and left God’s in ruins. The 1980s were a decade of earning and spending, and many Gen X children watched parents strap on the pouch for one more trip to one more mall. The fanny pack is innocent; the anxious grip on what is inside it is the thing worth examining. Treasure laid up on earth, Jesus warned, is subject to moth, rust, and thieves.

Traveling light. Jesus sent His disciples out without purse or scrip (Luk 10:4), and when He asked afterward whether they had lacked anything, they said, Nothing. The lesson was not that Christians must never carry a wallet — He later told them to take one — but that the Father provides. David’s scrip held five stones and a great faith (1Sa 17:40). The Christian’s best pack is the one Christ commands: bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not (Luk 12:33).
roots_summary: Middle Dutch pak → English pack; US informal fanny (the backside) → 1980s fanny pack (British bum bag) → 2010s belt bag; Scripture: bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33).
roots_lines: Middle Dutch pak → Middle English pakke — a bundle, a load to be carried
Early 20th-c. US informal fanny — the backside
1970s: belt pouches for skiers and hikers; mid-to-late 1980s: mass fashion
1990s: the tourist’s uniform and a fashion punchline; 2010s revival as the belt bag
Biblical bags: David’s scrip (1Sa 17:40); the bag with holes (Hag 1:6); bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33)
usage: "Honey, the sunscreen’s in the fanny pack."
David’s shepherd’s bag held five stones and a great faith (1Sa 17:40).
Provide yourselves bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33).

etymology: A trademark for the footbag, invented in Oregon City, Oregon, in 1972 by John Stalberger and Mike Marshall, who kicked a small handmade bean-filled bag as exercise while Stalberger recovered from knee surgery. Stalberger marketed it as the Hacky Sack and sold the rights to Wham-O in 1983. Through the 1980s and 1990s the hacky sack circle was a fixture of high-school parking lots, college quads, and concert grounds, and the name became generic for any footbag, with the verb to hack.
biblical_def: A hacky sack is a small, bean-filled footbag kept aloft with the feet, knees, and chest — never the hands — by a loose circle of players passing it around. In the 1980s and 90s it was everywhere: the high-school parking lot before first bell, the college quad, the grass outside a concert. The game has no winner. The point is to keep it up together, and when it drops, someone scoops it with a toe and the circle starts again. The Christian observation is that this is a surprisingly good picture of fellowship. Zechariah saw the restored Jerusalem with streets "full of boys and girls playing" (Zec 8:5); play belongs to the peace God gives. Solomon knew that "Two are better than one" (Ecc 4:9) and that "if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" (Ecc 4:10), which is what a hacky sack circle does every thirty seconds. Paul gives play its proper weight: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). The game is good, and it is not the main thing. He also held up the athlete as a model of discipline, a man "temperate in all things" for "a corruptible crown" (1Co 9:25), and asked how much more the Christian should strive for one that does not fade. The hacky sack circle also had a reputation as a hangout for the aimless and the class-skipping, and a father may need to say so. But the game itself is innocent. He can kick one around with his kids in the backyard and teach the lesson without a sermon: in the body of Christ nobody wins alone, and when the bag drops, you pick it up and keep it going together.
webster_summary: Trademark (Oregon, 1972; Wham-O, 1983) for the footbag kept aloft by a circle of players without hands; a harmless game that pictures fellowship — if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow (Ecc 4:10).
webster_full: HACKY SACK, n. (Gen X slang, trademark 1972, Oregon; generic by the late 1980s) A small bean- or pellet-filled footbag, kept in the air with the feet and body by a circle of players; the game itself. "Want to hack before class?"
Invented by John Stalberger and Mike Marshall in Oregon City, Oregon (1972); rights sold to Wham-O (1983); verb to hack.
The hacky sack circle: high-school lots, college quads, concert grounds; the competitive sport is called footbag.

Webster 1828: SACK, n. [Latin saccus. Heb. See the verb to sack] 1. A bag, usually a large cloth bag, used for holding and conveying corn, small wares, wool, cotton, hops, and the like. Genesis 42:25. …
Decode for parents: the game is innocent and cooperative; know who is in the circle, and kick one with your kids.
scriptures: Zec 8:5
And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
corruption_summary: The hacky sack is a harmless cooperative game whose circle was sometimes a gathering place for the aimless; Scripture blesses play and fellowship while reminding that bodily exercise profiteth little next to godliness.
corruption_paragraphs: The circle and its company. Nothing about kicking a bean bag is wrong, and plenty is right: exercise, laughter, a game where nobody loses. But in the 1980s and 90s the circle sometimes doubled as the gathering place for kids skipping class or drifting through school with no aim at all. Parents who saw it learned to ask not "what game is that?" but "who is in that circle?" The company a child keeps shapes him more than the game he plays. Watch the circle, not just the sack.

Keep it up together. The best thing about the game is its shape: no winner, no hands, everyone responsible for keeping it aloft, and when it drops, someone picks it up and starts again. Solomon’s two who are better than one (Ecc 4:9-10) would recognize it, and so would any healthy church. Paul puts play in its place, profitable a little (1Ti 4:8), and uses the athlete’s discipline to point to an incorruptible crown (1Co 9:25). A game can be a gift without becoming a god.
roots_summary: Hebrew saq → Latin saccus → English sack; Oregon City footbag (1972) → trademark Hacky Sack → Wham-O (1983) → the 1980s–90s circle; Scripture: two are better than one (Ecc 4:9).
roots_lines: Hebrew saq → Greek sakkos → Latin saccus → Old English sacc — a bag
1972: John Stalberger and Mike Marshall invent the footbag in Oregon City, Oregon
Hacky Sack trademark; rights sold to Wham-O in 1983
1980s–90s: the hacky sack circle on campuses and concert grounds; generic for any footbag
Biblical play and fellowship: boys and girls playing (Zec 8:5); one lifts up his fellow (Ecc 4:10)
usage: "Keep it up — we’re at forty kicks!"
If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow (Ecc 4:10) — the whole rule of the circle.
Bodily exercise profiteth little, but godliness is profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).

etymology: Clipped from vegetate (to live like a plant, without activity or thought), with out as in freak out and zone out; American teen and college slang by about 1980, and by the middle of the decade the standard Gen X phrase for collapsing in front of the television with no plan to move. The noun couch potato (c. 1976–79) names the same creature. Ironically, the Latin root vegetare meant to enliven.
biblical_def: To veg out is to do nothing on purpose: flop on the couch, turn on the television, and let the mind go as still as a vegetable. After a long week, Gen X called it a reward, and the remote control was its scepter. The Christian observation is that rest is good — God commanded it — but vegetating is not the same thing as resting. Jesus Himself told His tired disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mar 6:31), and He calls every weary sinner: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). True rest restores; it draws a man toward God and sends him back to his work refreshed. Vegging out, done every night, often does the opposite. Proverbs paints the slow slide: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep" (Pro 6:10), spoken to the sluggard who will not rise. And what fills the screen matters: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). The days are short and evil, so we are to be "Redeeming the time" (Eph 5:16). Stillness has its place — "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psa 46:10) — but that is stillness with a direction. A father can veg out with his kids on a rainy Saturday and enjoy it. He should also teach them the difference between a mind that rests in God and a mind that simply switches off, and model a Sabbath that is fuller than a couch.
webster_summary: American slang (c. 1980, from vegetate) for passive, mindless relaxation, classically before the television; Scripture commands real rest (Mar 6:31; Mat 11:28) but warns against the sluggard’s little folding of the hands (Pro 6:10).
webster_full: VEG OUT, v. (Gen X slang, c. 1980, American) To relax completely and passively, doing and thinking nothing, usually before a television. "I’m just going to veg out on the couch tonight."
Clipped from vegetate; also veg alone ("just vegging"); kin to zone out and chill.
Companion noun: couch potato (c. 1976–79); the remote control, common by the mid-1980s, as its emblem.

Webster 1828: VEGETATE, v.i. [Latin vegeto, vigeo, to flourish.] To sprout; to germinate; to grow; as plants; to grow and be enlarged by nutriment imbibed from the earth, air or water, by means of roots and leaves. …
Decode for parents: rest is God’s gift; teach the difference between a mind resting in God and a mind switched off.
scriptures: Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Pro 6:10
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep:
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
corruption_summary: Veg out confuses rest with vacancy; Scripture commands real rest in Christ and real stillness before God, and warns that a little folding of the hands becomes the sluggard’s way of life.
corruption_paragraphs: Vacancy is not rest. The word itself is honest: to vegetate is to live like a plant. The television age taught a generation that the reward for work is to stop being a person for a few hours. But God’s rest is not emptiness; it is fullness — worship, fellowship, sleep, a walk, a meal with family. A man can veg out every evening and wake more tired, because a mind fed only on screens is not restored. The sluggard’s little folding of the hands (Pro 6:10) never feels like a decision; it simply becomes a life.

Be still, and know. Scripture’s stillness has an object: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psa 46:10). Christ’s call to rest is a call to Himself (Mat 11:28), and His invitation to the disciples to rest a while (Mar 6:31) came after hard labor. Christians should rest more deeply than the world, not less — and they should guard what goes before their eyes while they do (Psa 101:3), redeeming even their leisure (Eph 5:16). The couch is not the enemy; the empty mind is.
roots_summary: Latin vegetare (to enliven) → English vegetate (to live like a plant) → American veg out (c. 1980) → the couch-potato age; Scripture: come unto me … and I will give you rest (Mat 11:28).
roots_lines: Latin vegetare — to enliven, to quicken; vegetus, lively
English vegetate — to grow as plants do; later, to live idly without thought
c. 1980: American teen and college slang veg out
1980s: cable television and the remote control make it a nightly habit
Biblical rest: rest a while (Mar 6:31); be still, and know (Psa 46:10)
usage: "No homework tonight — I’m going to veg out."
Come ye yourselves apart … and rest a while (Mar 6:31) — rest with the Master.
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber (Pro 6:10): the slow way vegging becomes sloth.

etymology: Coined by First Lady Nancy Reagan in 1982, during a visit to an elementary school in Oakland, California, when a schoolgirl asked what she should do if someone offered her drugs and Mrs. Reagan answered that she should just say no. The phrase named the national anti-drug campaign of the 1980s, with school Just Say No clubs, public-service announcements, and rallies; later critics found it too simple, comedians parodied it, and it survives as shorthand for any flat refusal.
biblical_def: Just Say No was the anti-drug slogan of the Gen X childhood: on posters, buttons, school assemblies, and Saturday-morning commercials. It began with a simple exchange in 1982, when a schoolgirl in Oakland asked Nancy Reagan what to do if someone offered her drugs, and the First Lady told her to just say no. Later critics mocked the slogan as naive. The Christian observation is that it was simple because it was true, and Solomon said it first: "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" (Pro 1:10). Joseph just said no in Potiphar’s house: "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Gen 39:9). Daniel "purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself" (Dan 1:8). And God promises that every temptation comes with "a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it" (1Co 10:13). Where the slogan fell short was not in its content but in its power source. A boy cannot say no to sin for long on willpower and a poster. The New Testament supplies what the campaign could not: "the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men" (Tit 2:11), "Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world" (Tit 2:12). Grace teaches the no. A father can teach his children the old slogan without embarrassment; then he should give them the reason and the strength behind it: the Christ who said no to every temptation in our place, and who gives His Spirit to say it in us.
webster_summary: Nancy Reagan’s anti-drug slogan (Oakland, 1982) and the campaign it named; simple and true — Solomon said it first, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not (Pro 1:10) — and grace supplies the strength to keep saying it (Tit 2:12).
webster_full: JUST SAY NO, interj. and phrase (Gen X slang, 1982, Oakland, California) Refuse drugs, alcohol, or any temptation flatly, without debate. "If someone offers you drugs, just say no."
Coined in Nancy Reagan’s answer to a schoolgirl’s question at an Oakland school (1982); name of the 1980s national campaign and its school clubs.
Later used ironically and as shorthand for any blunt refusal; parodied in 1990s comedy.
No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is a 1982 American campaign slogan.
Decode for parents: the slogan is true but needs a power source; teach the no, and the grace that teaches it.
scriptures: Pro 1:10
My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.
Gen 39:9
There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?
Dan 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
corruption_summary: Just Say No was simple and true, but a slogan cannot supply what it commands; Scripture gives the same counsel and adds the grace of God that teaches us to deny ungodliness.
corruption_paragraphs: Willpower on a poster. The campaign was right about the answer and thin on the reason. Children were told to refuse but seldom told why the refusal mattered or where the strength to keep refusing would come from. When the posters came down and the pressure went up, many found that a slogan was no match for a hungry heart and a persuasive friend. The world’s later mockery of the phrase did not make it false; it exposed that moral rules without a living Savior run out of fuel.

The no that grace teaches. Scripture’s refusals are grounded in a Person. Joseph refused because the sin was "against God" (Gen 39:9); Daniel because he had purposed in his heart (Dan 1:8). The apostle says the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts (Tit 2:12), and that God is faithful to provide a way to escape (1Co 10:13). Teach the slogan; then teach the gospel that makes it livable: Christ said no to every temptation in our place and gives His Spirit to say it in us.
